### Problem: Another Sorting Problem {#sec-lts-p6-a}

::: {.p-statement}
There are $n$ pairwise distinct strings $s_1, \dots, s_n$, each of length exactly $m$, over the uppercase letters `A`–`Z` ($1 \le n \cdot m \le 10^6$). Sort them in **asc-desc-ending** order: to compare two strings, find the first position where they differ; at an **odd** position (1-indexed) the string with the earlier letter comes first, at an **even** position the string with the *later* letter comes first. Print the original indices in sorted order.

Source: [CF 1575A · Another Sorting Problem](https://codeforces.com/problemset/problem/1575/A){.solved rating="1100"}

Example — $n = 5$, $m = 2$, strings `AA AB BB BA AZ`. Output `5 2 1 3 4`: the `A…` strings come first (position 1 ascending), and among them `AZ, AB, AA` (position 2 descending); then `BB, BA`.
:::

::: {.p-intuition}
All keys have the same length $m$ over a 26-letter alphabet: that is exactly the shape LSD radix sort was made for (@sec-lts-a3). Flip every even column's letter ($c \mapsto 25 - c$) so that every column sorts ascending, then run one **stable** counting sort per column, from the last column to the first. No two strings are ever compared; the work is $O(m(n + 26)) = O(nm)$, linear in the size of the input.
:::

::: {.p-approach}
1. **Comparison sort on a transformed key.** Map each string to a tuple whose even-position letters are negated, and sort the indices by that tuple. $O(nm\log n)$ time: each of the $O(n\log n)$ comparisons may read up to $m$ letters.
2. **LSD radix sort.** Keep a list of indices, initially $1..n$. For $j = m, m-1, \dots, 1$: stable counting sort of the list by the digit of column $j$ (the letter for odd $j$, $25$ minus the letter for even $j$). After the pass on column 1, the list is the answer. $O(m(n + 26))$ time, $O(n)$ extra space.

**Invariant.** After the passes on columns $j..m$, the list is sorted by the suffix of columns $j..m$ in the asc-desc order. The pass on column $j - 1$ orders by that column and, being stable, keeps the suffix order among strings that tie on it, so the invariant extends one column to the left (the induction of @sec-lts-a3).
:::

The buttons are in order. Each one keeps the previous solution and changes only what that form changes.

::: {.panel-tabset .solution-forms}

#### Comparison sort on a key

::: {.form-next}
Turn the custom order into an ordinary tuple order: keep odd-position letters, negate even-position letters, and let the library sort compare tuples. Correct and short, at $O(nm\log n)$.

**Worked example.** `AA → (65, -65)`, `AB → (65, -66)`, `AZ → (65, -90)`, `BA → (66, -65)`, `BB → (66, -66)`. Ascending tuples: `AZ, AB, AA, BB, BA`, that is indices `5 2 1 3 4`.
:::

::: {.panel-tabset group="lang"}
##### Python

```{python}
def as1575_sort(strs):
    def key(i):
        return tuple(ord(c) if j % 2 == 0 else -ord(c) for j, c in enumerate(strs[i]))
    return [i + 1 for i in sorted(range(len(strs)), key=key)]
```

##### C++

```cpp
#include <bits/stdc++.h>
using namespace std;

int main() {
    int n, m;
    scanf("%d %d", &n, &m);
    vector<string> s(n);
    static char buf[1000005];
    for (auto& x : s) { scanf("%s", buf); x = buf; }
    for (auto& x : s)
        for (int j = 1; j < m; j += 2) x[j] = (char)('A' + 'Z' - x[j]);   // flip even columns
    vector<int> idx(n);
    iota(idx.begin(), idx.end(), 0);
    sort(idx.begin(), idx.end(), [&](int a, int b) { return s[a] < s[b]; });
    for (int i : idx) printf("%d ", i + 1);
    puts("");
}
```
:::

**Reading it line by line.** In 0-indexed code the problem's odd positions are $j = 0, 2, 4, \dots$, so the C++ flips $j = 1, 3, \dots$ and then uses plain string comparison. Each comparison reads up to $m$ letters, and with $n\cdot m = 10^6$ this is fast enough on the judge; the point of the next form is that it never needs to compare at all.

#### LSD radix sort

::: {.form-next}
Swap the comparison sort for $m$ stable counting-sort passes, last column first, each over a 26-slot histogram. The flip $c \mapsto 25 - c$ on even columns makes every pass an ordinary ascending counting sort. $O(m(n + 26))$.

**Worked example.** Pass on column 2 (flipped, so `Z` is smallest): `AZ, AB, BB, AA, BA`. Pass on column 1, stable: the `A`s keep their order `AZ, AB, AA`, then `BB, BA`. Indices `5 2 1 3 4`.
:::

::: {#fig-lts-1575-passes}

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| renderings: [light, dark]
def draw(ax, p):
    strs = ["AA", "AB", "BB", "BA", "AZ"]
    order = list(range(len(strs)))
    rows = [dict(values=[strs[i] for i in order], label="input", note="indices 1..5")]
    for j in range(len(strs[0]) - 1, -1, -1):
        dig = lambda i: (ord(strs[i][j]) - 65) if j % 2 == 0 else 25 - (ord(strs[i][j]) - 65)
        order = sorted(order, key=dig)                       # Python's sort is stable
        rows.append(dict(values=[strs[i] for i in order],
                         label=f"by column {j + 1}",
                         note=("descending letter" if j % 2 else "ascending letter") + ", stable",
                         colors={k: ("amber" if j % 2 else "green") for k in range(len(order))}))
    assert [i + 1 for i in order] == [5, 2, 1, 3, 4]
    V.trace(ax, p, rows, gap=2.4)
V.show(draw)
```

LSD radix on the sample: one stable pass per column, the last column first. The second pass sorts by the first letter only; the three `A…` strings tie there, so stability keeps the order that the column-2 pass gave them.

:::

::: {.panel-tabset group="lang"}
##### Python

```{python}
#| label: arr-lts-1575-radix
def as1575_radix(strs):
    n, m = len(strs), len(strs[0])
    order = list(range(n))
    for j in range(m - 1, -1, -1):                 # last column first
        def dig(i):
            d = ord(strs[i][j]) - 65
            return d if j % 2 == 0 else 25 - d     # even positions (1-indexed) descend
        cnt = [0] * 27
        for i in order:
            cnt[dig(i) + 1] += 1
        for d in range(26):
            cnt[d + 1] += cnt[d]                   # cnt[d] = first slot of digit d
        out = [0] * n
        for i in order:                            # left to right: stable
            d = dig(i)
            out[cnt[d]] = i
            cnt[d] += 1
        order = out
    return [i + 1 for i in order]

for _ in range(300):
    m = random.randint(1, 4)
    want = random.randint(1, 15)
    pool = set()
    while len(pool) < min(want, 4 ** m):
        pool.add("".join(random.choice("ABCZ") for _ in range(m)))
    strs = list(pool)
    random.shuffle(strs)
    assert as1575_radix(strs) == as1575_sort(strs)
assert as1575_radix(["AA", "AB", "BB", "BA", "AZ"]) == [5, 2, 1, 3, 4]
print("as1575_radix OK")
```

##### C++

```cpp
#include <bits/stdc++.h>
using namespace std;

int main() {
    int n, m;
    scanf("%d %d", &n, &m);
    vector<string> s(n);
    static char buf[1000005];
    for (auto& x : s) { scanf("%s", buf); x = buf; }
    vector<int> order(n), out(n);
    iota(order.begin(), order.end(), 0);
    for (int j = m - 1; j >= 0; --j) {               // last column first
        int cnt[27] = {0};
        auto dig = [&](int i) { int d = s[i][j] - 'A'; return j % 2 == 0 ? d : 25 - d; };
        for (int i : order) ++cnt[dig(i) + 1];
        for (int d = 0; d < 26; ++d) cnt[d + 1] += cnt[d];
        for (int i : order) out[cnt[dig(i)]++] = i;  // stable placement
        order.swap(out);
    }
    for (int i : order) printf("%d ", i + 1);
    puts("");
}
```
:::

**Reading it line by line.** This pass uses *start* positions and a left-to-right scan, the mirror of the end-position, right-to-left scan of @sec-lts-a2; both are stable. The list being sorted holds indices, not strings, so each pass moves $n$ integers rather than $n$ strings of length $m$. The stress test draws from only four letters so that many strings share prefixes and the tie-keeping of each pass really matters.

:::

::: {.p-complexity}
**Comparison sort on a key** is $O(nm\log n)$ time in the worst case. **LSD radix sort** is $O(m(n + 26))$ time, which is $O(nm)$, linear in the input size, and $O(n)$ extra space besides the strings.
:::

::: {.p-edge}
- $m = 1$: a single counting-sort pass on the only column.
- $n = 1$: every pass leaves the one index in place; output `1`.
- Strings are distinct, so the order is total; if they were not, the stable passes would print equal strings in input order.
:::

- [LC 1985 · Find the Kth Largest Integer in the Array](https://leetcode.com/problems/find-the-kth-largest-integer-in-the-array/){difficulty="Medium"} — strings of digits of *different* lengths: bucket by length first (an MSD step), then radix within one length.
- [LC 937 · Reorder Data in Log Files](https://leetcode.com/problems/reorder-data-in-log-files/){difficulty="Medium"} — a multi-key order on strings, the comparison-sort side of the same idea.
:::
